sweep_summary: Single works with stress in the title: Ikeda 2002 (LTBA 25.2, pp. 27-45), the only stress/accent-keyword title Glottolog lists for west2417 and already in the per-language bibliography. It was already held by the project from the 9/16 download (sealang scan, no text, scanned); I re-read the full scanned and checked the two deciding pages (33, 36) against the page scan. It is a first-hand analysis of exactly this variety (western dialect, Sade district) and argues Munya's suprasegmentals are a location-contrastive pitch accent (one lexically marked H syllable per word, unmarked L elsewhere; /L H/ the default pattern and the only one for prefix+stem verbs; rising/falling = phrase-final intonation; no spreading), with no stress rule stated. This CONFIRMS the catalog's 'tonal' (tonal-OR-pitch accent, no stress) coding from Bai 2019, whose sec. 2.4 explicitly builds on and agrees with Ikeda 2002 for disyllabic patterns; Bai 2019 (full grammar, 2019, same dialect) remains the better deciding source, so no supersession. Side check outside the item list: Gao 2015 EHESS thesis (cited by Bai as the other pitch accent analysis) has only a theses.fr record with no full text ('deux schemes tonaux selon la position du ton H' in the abstract); nothing left to acquire at priority above none.fr.

new_statements.quote: Now turning our attention to the correspondence between HUANG's and IKEDA's transcription of each word form, we see that only the high position of the pitch is in consistent correspondence. On the other hand, the non-high position does not mean [+low] but [-high], and any pitch may appear. Thus all we need to do is to indicate in the lexicon the position in each word bearing the high pitch. [p. 33] ... (3) /L//H/ > [33][55] or [33][53]# ... I have found that this is the default pitch pattern for all classes of words in Mu-nya. And we can observe that all the verbs (prefix + verb stem) display the /L//H/ pitch pattern. [p. 36]

new_statements.reading: First-hand fieldwork analysis of Western Munya word prosody as a lexical pitch accent system: each word carries at most one lexically specified high-pitch (accent) position, contrastive by location (H vs unmarked L; /H L/ vs /L H/ in disyllables), with /L H/ (final-H) the statistical default for all word classes and obligatory for prefix+stem verbs; rising/falling contours are phrase-final intonation, not tonemes; no pitch spreading. No stress is described. This supports the catalog's 'tonal' (tonal-OR-pitch accent, no stress rule) coding and adds the refinement that the accent position is lexically free but defaults to the final syllable in disyllables.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all segments of the deciding quotation and the domain quote are verbatim in the extracted text we hold of Bai 2019 at the stated sections/pages (2.4.1-2.4.2 pp. 55-58 with Table 2.5; 2.10 p. 64); 'stress' is absent from the grammar. (2) Deciding source is a 2019 open-access reference grammar (JCU PhD, ~546 pp PDF) on the correct languoid (western dialect), the newest and fullest description in Glottolog's 9-item list; it reviews and supersedes the earlier tonal analyses. (3) The one dedicated phonology article (Ikeda 2002, LTBA) was downloaded from the open sealang archive, scanned, and read: it argues Mu-nya prosody is a location-contrastive pitch accent (marked H vs unmarked L), with no stress rule, confirming tonal-OR-pitch accent with empty rule string. Gao 2015's theses.fr abstract (H/L underlying tones; H-position schemes in polysyllables) also agrees; full text is library-only

sources.citation: Ikeda, Takumi. 2002. On pitch accent in the Mu-nya language. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 25(2): 27-45.
sources.quote: Thus all we need to do is to indicate in the lexicon the position in each word bearing the high pitch. [...] So we can recognize that the basic mechanism driving the prosody of Mu-nya is to indicate the location of marking of the words in their lexicon: "where is high point?" or "which syllable is marked?" It is not a mechanism wherein each syllable chooses which melody it will bear. (p. 33) [...] Monosyllabic words with accent appear with high pitch, while those without accent appear, in contrast, with low pitch. (p. 35) [...] (3) /L//H/ > [33][55] or [33][53]# [...] I have found that this is the default pitch pattern for all classes of words in Mu-nya. And we can observe that all the verbs (prefix + verb stem) display the /L//H/ pitch pattern. (p. 36)
sources.locator: sec. 2.4 'Tone or Accent' p. 33; sec. 3.1 'Monosyllabic Words' p. 35; sec. 3.2 'Disyllabic Words' pp. 35-37; sec. 4 'How to indicate the accent in the lexicon' pp. 39-41; Appendix 'Spreading' pp. 41-42
sources.note: Explicitly on the western dialect (Sade district; p. 27). Argues the four surface 'tones' [55 53 35 33] are not tonemes: the only contrastive property is the LOCATION of a high-pitch accent /H/ (marked) vs unmarked low [33]; rising [35] and falling [53] are non-distinctive phrase-final/isolation intonation ([55]>[53] and [33]>[35] before pause, p. 35). Word patterns: monosyllables /H/ vs /L/; disyllables /H H/ (rare, mostly Tibetan loans), /H L/ (few nouns, no verbs), /L H/ = 'the default pitch pattern for all classes of words', all prefix+stem verbs /L H/; */L L/ unattested; tri-/quadrisylla…

sources.citation: Gao, Yang. 2015. Description de la langue Menya: phonologie et syntaxe. These de doctorat, EHESS Paris (dir. L. Sagart, G. Jacques). NNT 2015EHES0181.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.quote: Abstract: 'deux tons (H et L) au niveau sous-jacent pour les monosyllabiques' which neutralize in citation form, and 'deux schemes tonaux selon la position du ton H sur la premiere ou la deuxieme syllabe d'un mot plurisyllabique'. Western Menya dialect. Consistent with Bai's report of Gao (2015:77-81) and with a lexical H/L word-tone (pitch-accent) system; no stress mentioned in abstract.
sources.note: The only other full grammar in Glottolog (494 pp, phonology-first); its pp. 77-81 tonal analysis is the one Bai 2019 builds on and partly revises (Gao lacks /HH/, /LLH/). Would give an independent primary statement of the H/L word-tone system; abstract already agrees, so it would corroborate rather than change the classification.
